newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Internal Samsung report sparks Kia Motors' wrath.
newsitem.headline: Internal Samsung report sparks Kia Motors' wrath.

text.p: Kia Motors Corp, launching another round in South Korea's car wars, said on Thursday it would take legal action against Samsung Motors for a leaked internal report suggesting Kia was having management problems.

"Samsung's report seems to be designed to measure public opinion about its intention to take over Kia. That must be very irritating for Kia because it is a life-and-death issue," said Hur Kang, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Kia Motors said on Thursday it planned legal action against Samsung Motors Inc for disseminating what is said was false information about Kia, one of South Korea's three leading car makers.

"We will seek legal compensation for expected huge losses and the damage to our reputation that the false information could cause, and we plan to file a complaint with the prosecution office," Kia said in a statement.
Kia said Samsung argued in an internal report that confidence in Kia's top managers had been lost and that Kia faced "internal managerial conflicts".
The Samsung report also said Kia had reached its maximum growth potential, Kia said.
"All these arguments are totally groundless," the Kia statement said.

Kia said Samsung's contention that the vehicle industry should be anchored by companies operating under stable group management was an effort to win support for Samsung's hostile takeover intentions towards Kia, the only car maker not affiliated with a large diversified business conglomerate.
A Samsung Motor spokesman acknowledged the existence of the internal report but said he could not comment.
"The report does not represent Samsung's official position," said spokesman Han Sang-yoon.

Samsung has never admitted its intention to take over Kia, but industry observers and analysts said Samsung would be interested in such a deal because it would greatly help Samsung's expansion into the car industry.
"Samsung's entry was quite problematic because it would add to the already expected over-supply of South Korea's car industry," said Kim Byung-joon, an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
"It could drag all car makers into a mud-wrestling match if Samsung continues to expand."
Domestic car sales have slumped in recent months as the economy has slowed, revealing a potentially serious over-supply problem.
"But the government is more to blame for its inconsistent policies," Kim said.

The government initially said it would not allow Samsung to manufacturer passenger cars because of fears of excess capacity. But it later changed its mind, persuaded by the possible benefits of competition.
The Samsung Group won a government licence to build cars in a technical tie-up with Japan's Nissan Motor Co in 1994 to enter South Korea's already crowded automobile industry.
Samsung Motors plans to produce 80,000 vehicles in 1998, with the annual output rising to 250,000 units in 1999 and 500,000 units in 2002.
Analysts said Samsung's entry could help strengthen South Korea's car industry through heated competition, which this year resulted in the introduction of several popular models.
